title: Dynamic Programming, Part 3: APSP, Parens, Piano
note: Four chunks, each unusually long (227, 193, 168, and 27 lines), because this transcript has almost no speaker changes — only three brief audience questions in 615 lines — and lesson.mjs only starts a new chunk at a column-0 line, so long stretches of uninterrupted monologue stay in one chunk rather than being split near the usual ~38-line target. sections.topic: ERIK DEMAINE: All right. Welcome back to 006 and our dynamic programming
sections.emphasis: This is a long stretch with three distinct payoffs — a SRTBOT recap, two old algorithms reframed as dynamic programs, and a brand-new one — so keep the arc visible. Open with the day's theme, named at the end of the previous lecture: subproblem expansion, adding constraints to a subproblem so it 'remembers' more context, at the cost of multiplying how many subproblems exist. Recap SRTBOT briskly: for sequence problems, prefer prefix or suffix subproblems over substrings when possible (fewer of them); the relation comes from a well-chosen question — for suffixes, ask about the first item; for prefixes, the last — and answer it by local brute force, trying every possible answer and recursing (equivalently, 'guess' the answer and assume it's right, understanding that the guessing is really a loop when you analyze the running time); then check acyclicity, fix a topological order, write base cases, and total the running time as subproblems times non-recursive work per subproblem. Reframe DAG relaxation as exactly this pattern: the subproblem is δ(s, v), the question guessed is 'what is the last edge (u, v) on a shortest path?', and the recurrence takes a minimum over all incoming edges — correct only because the graph is a DAG, so the call graph has no cycles; on a general graph this recursion would never terminate. Then reframe Bellman-Ford the same way, and land why it needed something DAG relaxation didn't: define δ_k(s, v) as the shortest-path weight using at most k edges — a subproblem expansion by k — and observe that this specific constraint is what makes the recurrence acyclic even though the underlying graph has cycles, since every reference from δ_k always points to δ_(k−1). Total cost: O(VE) via V subproblem-counts times E average incoming-edge cost, the same VE bound as before, just derived from a min instead of relaxation. Finally, introduce today's genuinely new algorithm, Floyd-Warshall, for all-pairs shortest paths: define d(u, v, k) as the shortest u-to-v path using only intermediate vertices numbered 1 through k (vertices are pre-numbered for this purpose) — a different kind of subproblem expansion than δ_k's edge-count limit. State the recurrence and why it's cheap: d(u, v, k) = min(d(u, v, k−1), d(u, k, k−1) + d(k, v, k−1)) — either the shortest path avoids vertex k entirely (first term), or it passes through k exactly once, in which case (assuming no negative-weight cycles) it must reach k and then leave k using only smaller-numbered intermediates on each half. This recurrence has only two choices, so it costs O(1) non-recursive work per subproblem, and there are O(V³) subproblems (V choices each for u, v, and k), giving O(V³) total — worse than V·E for sparse graphs, but for dense graphs (E close to V²), this matches V·E while being dramatically simpler code: a base case at k=0 (either 0, the edge weight, or infinity, depending on whether u=v or an edge exists) and a straightforward triple loop over k, u, v in increasing k order.

quiz.question: Floyd-Warshall's recurrence is d(u,v,k) = min(d(u,v,k−1), d(u,k,k−1) + d(k,v,k−1)). What do the two terms inside this minimum represent?
options: The first term is the shortest u-to-v path that doesn't use vertex k as an intermediate at all; the second is the shortest path that does pass through k, split into a u-to-k leg and a k-to-v leg, each restricted to intermediates numbered less than k
The first term is the shortest path using an even number of intermediate vertices, and the second is the shortest path using an odd number
The two terms represent the shortest path found by Dijkstra and by Bellman-Ford respectively, and the algorithm picks whichever ran faster
quiz.explain: The subproblem d(u,v,k) is defined as the shortest u-to-v path restricted to using only vertices numbered 1 through k as intermediates. Adding vertex k to that allowed set means exactly two things can happen: either the optimal path still doesn't need k (so it's identical to d(u,v,k−1), the first term), or it benefits from routing through k exactly once, splitting into a u-to-k leg and a k-to-v leg that (under the no-negative-cycle assumption) each only need intermediates less than k — exactly d(u,k,k−1) + d(k,v,k−1), the second term. Taking the smaller of these two options is what makes each subproblem cost only constant non-recursive work, despite there being a cubic number of subproblems overall.

sections.topic: AUDIENCE: So how does this this compare to just running Dijkstra's algor
sections.emphasis: Open by answering the audience's comparison question precisely, since it sets the right mental model for when to reach for which algorithm: running Dijkstra V times (which is Johnson's algorithm's running time, after its one Bellman-Ford pass to handle negative edges) costs roughly V² log V for sparse graphs, better than Floyd-Warshall's flat V³ — but for dense graphs, where E approaches V², Johnson's own VE term already costs V³, so there's no asymptotic advantage left, and Floyd-Warshall wins on simplicity. State the practical rule Demaine lands on: if you know ahead of time that your graph is sparse or you have negative weights with room to benefit from sparsity, use Johnson's; if it's dense, or you don't especially care about being optimal, Floyd-Warshall's simplicity is worth the flat V³. Close the graphs unit by re-framing what just happened: Floyd-Warshall's u, v, k subproblem — 'shortest path using vertex-numbered prefix 1 through k as intermediates' — is secretly a familiar idea, a prefix subproblem, just over the vertex-numbering rather than over an input sequence. Then pivot entirely to a new domain: arithmetic parenthesization. Define the problem precisely: given a formula like a0 ⋆1 a1 ⋆2 a2 ⋯ ⋆(n−1) a(n−1), where each ⋆i is plus or times, choose how to parenthesize it (any valid binary expression tree over the same sequence of operators) to maximize the result. Walk Demaine's worked example, 7 + 4 × 3 + 5, evaluating to 88 under the best parenthesization rather than the 'obvious' order-of-operations reading. Explain carefully why the natural first instinct — prefix and suffix subproblems — fails: guessing the root of the expression tree (the last operator evaluated) splits the sequence into a left piece and a right piece, but as you recurse into either piece and guess ITS root, you get a prefix of a suffix — a substring — so mixing prefixes and suffixes forces substrings anyway; the subproblems have to be substrings from the start. Then introduce the second twist, subproblem expansion by optimization direction: maximizing a sum only ever needs the max of its two parts, but maximizing a PRODUCT can require the MINIMUM of a part, because the product of two very negative numbers is very positive — walk Demaine's example with negative numbers (7 + (−4) × 3 + (−5)) where the best parenthesization deliberately makes a sub-expression as negative as possible so that a later multiplication flips it positive. So the subproblem has to track both a minimum and a maximum for every substring: define x(i, j, opt), for opt ∈ {min, max}, as the optimal value achievable on the substring a_i ⋆(i+1) ⋯ ⋆(j−1) a_(j−1). Write the recurrence: guess which operator ⋆k (for i < k < j) is evaluated last, splitting into x(i, k, optL) and x(k, j, optR) combined by ⋆k; brute-force all four combinations of optL, optR ∈ {min, max}, since which combination is right depends on the signs involved and isn't worth reasoning about case-by-case. Base case: single-element substrings, x(i, i+1, opt) = a_i regardless of opt, since there's nothing to optimize over. Topological order: increasing substring length (j − i), since every recursive call is to a strictly shorter substring. Total cost: O(n²) substrings times 2 for the min/max split, times O(n) choices of k per substring (a constant number of optL/optR combinations), giving O(n³) — polynomial, despite there being exponentially many (about 4ⁿ) possible parenthesizations to implicitly search.

quiz.question: Why does the arithmetic-parenthesization DP need to compute BOTH the minimum and maximum achievable value for every substring, rather than just the maximum (which is ultimately what's asked for)?
options: Multiplying two negative numbers gives a positive result, so the best way to maximize a product sub-expression can require first making one of its parts as negative (as minimal) as possible — a maximum-only subproblem could never discover that option
It is only necessary when the formula contains subtraction or division, not for plain plus and times
Tracking both min and max is purely a performance optimization; correctness only requires the max subproblem
quiz.explain: Demaine's worked example makes this concrete: with negative numbers present, the parenthesization that achieves the overall maximum deliberately makes one sub-expression as negative as possible, because multiplying two very negative numbers produces a large positive result. A DP that only ever tracked 'the maximum achievable on this substring' would never surface that minimizing sub-choice as an option, and would silently return a wrong, smaller answer. Tracking min alongside max is exactly the subproblem expansion this lecture's theme is about — a deliberate multiplication of the subproblem space to remember something the recurrence genuinely needs, not a mere speed trick.

sections.topic: AUDIENCE: Would anything go wrong if I added minus or divide?
sections.emphasis: Open with the audience's extension question and give it a careful, honest answer rather than a quick yes: subtraction is fine, since negating a range is simple and behaves like addition's case, needing only the extremes of each side. Division is trickier — the real requirement, which Demaine names precisely, is that computing the max or min of an operation from two input ranges only ever needs to plug in the EXTREME endpoints of those ranges (a kind of interval arithmetic), and for division that isn't quite enough near zero — you also need to know how close to zero each side can get, adding two more tracked quantities (four total, instead of two), which would multiply the subproblem space by 4 instead of 2, but the framework still works. Note Demaine's aside for what this teaches generally: dynamic programming doesn't require cleverness about the operator itself, just an honest local brute force over whatever quantities the recurrence actually needs — figuring out what those quantities are is the real skill. Then pivot to the lecture's last problem, piano (and later guitar) fingering, a genuine real-world application. Define it precisely: given a sequence of notes t_0, ..., t_(n−1) to be played on an F-fingered hand, and a difficulty function d(t, f, t′, f′) giving the cost of playing note t with finger f immediately followed by note t′ with finger f′, choose a finger assignment f_0, ..., f_(n−1) minimizing the total transition difficulty. Explain why the natural suffix subproblem — 'the best way to play the suffix starting at note i' — isn't quite enough on its own: because the difficulty function needs to know BOTH the current finger and the next finger simultaneously, a suffix subproblem that doesn't also record which finger it starts on can't be correctly plugged into that function when it's called from the previous note. So expand the subproblem by the starting finger: x(i, f) = minimum total difficulty to play the suffix starting at note i, given that finger f plays note t_i. Write the recurrence: x(i, f) = min over f′ (the next finger) of x(i+1, f′) + d(t_i, f, t_(i+1), f′) — guessing only the very next finger, since x(i+1, f′) already commits to and accounts for f′ being used at position i+1. Solve the original problem by minimizing x(0, f) over all F choices of starting finger. Total cost: O(nF) subproblems, O(F) work each (trying every next finger), giving O(nF²) — linear in n, and fast whenever F is a small constant (5, for a human hand). Close by noting how naturally this generalizes: to multiple simultaneous notes (chords), the subproblem's 'state' becomes which F fingers are on which of up to F simultaneous notes, costing a constant (if large) multiplier per subproblem; and the exact same framework transfers to guitar fingering, where the finger-reach difficulty function is defined the same way.

quiz.question: In the piano-fingering DP, why does the subproblem x(i, f) need to record the starting finger f, rather than just being 'the best way to play the suffix starting at note i'?
options: The transition-difficulty function d(t, f, t′, f′) needs to know both the current note's finger and the next note's finger at the same time; a suffix-only subproblem, called from the previous note, would have no way to supply which finger it was told to start with
It's purely a speed optimization — tracking the finger lets the algorithm skip redundant recursive calls, but a suffix-only version would still give the correct answer, just more slowly
The finger only needs to be tracked when playing chords (multiple simultaneous notes), not for the single-note case described first
quiz.explain: The whole difficulty of this problem is that transition cost depends on a PAIR of fingers — the one leaving the current note and the one arriving at the next note. When note i's subproblem is called from note i−1's recurrence, the caller needs to plug a specific finger into d(t_(i−1), f, t_i, f′) — and the only way to guarantee x(i, f′) actually reflects a solution that starts with finger f′ on note i is to bake that finger into the subproblem's definition. Without it, there would be no way to correctly compute the transition cost between notes i−1 and i at all — this is a correctness requirement, not a speed one, and it's exactly the same 'subproblem expansion to remember state' theme that ran through Bellman-Ford's k, Floyd-Warshall's k, and the parenthesization problem's min/max.

sections.emphasis: The audience turn here is inaudible in the transcript, but from Demaine's reply it's clearly a request to name a favorite song — 'Super Mario Brothers, my favorite song' — and he uses it to close the lecture with a live, informal illustration of the piano-fingering framework applied to guitar. Walk it loosely, in the spirit it's given: a real guitar note can often be played on more than one string, so the fingering problem gains a second decision (which string, not just which finger), each choice with its own difficulty trade-offs — an open string is easier than a fretted one, a small reach is easier than a stretch, and a transition that lets a nearby finger stay in a convenient position is easier than one that doesn't. Demaine narrates his own on-the-spot choices this way: starting on an open string for ease, then choosing an index finger for the first note because it's easiest and leaves the pinky free to reach further notes later, then a middle finger for the next note as a small, comfortable reach. Land the closing point of the whole lecture on this note: the entire day's throughline — DAG shortest paths, Bellman-Ford's edge-count expansion, Floyd-Warshall's vertex-prefix expansion, parenthesization's min/max expansion, and piano fingering's starting-finger expansion — is one repeated move, subproblem expansion: whenever a recurrence needs to know some extra piece of 'state' to be computed correctly, multiply the subproblem space by however many values that state can take, as long as that multiplier stays small (a constant, or something polynomial), and the local-brute-force machinery of SRTBOT handles the rest without needing any new cleverness about the problem itself.

quiz.question: Demaine closes the lecture by naming subproblem expansion as the common thread across DAG shortest paths, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, parenthesization, and piano fingering. What is the general move he's describing?
options: Whenever a recurrence needs some extra piece of information to be computed correctly (an edge budget, an allowed-vertex prefix, an optimization direction, a starting finger), multiply the subproblem space by however many values that extra state can take, keeping the multiplier small — a constant or low-degree polynomial — so the SRTBOT machinery still runs efficiently
Always convert graph problems into sequence problems by first running a topological sort, regardless of what the recurrence actually needs
Replace every use of memoization with a bottom-up table whenever the subproblem count exceeds a few hundred, to avoid recursion overhead
quiz.explain: Each example in the lecture adds exactly one dimension to its subproblems because the natural, unexpanded version of the recurrence couldn't be answered correctly otherwise: Bellman-Ford needed an edge-count bound to break cycles in the recursion; Floyd-Warshall needed a vertex-numbering prefix to turn an expensive degree-sized loop into a cheap constant-sized one; parenthesization needed both min and max because products can flip sign; piano fingering needed the starting finger because the difficulty function is defined on a pair of fingers at once. In every case the fix is the same: multiply the subproblem count by the size of whatever state needs remembering, and as long as that multiplier is small, the overall running time (subproblem count times work per subproblem) stays polynomial.
